children: network of Southeast Asian cloud partners has helped Chinese companies access advanced AI computing despite U.S. restrictions on direct chip exports, The Wall Street Journal reported. That business faces growing pressure as Washington considers tighter controls following Jensen Huang’s ouster as chief executive.
For investors, the scrutiny creates uncertainty over Nvidia’s

overseas revenue and billions of dollars committed to regional data centers. Restrictions on Chinese customers could weaken demand, complicate financing and leave operators seeking replacement tenants.
Chinese companies can legally rent Nvidia-powered

computing capacity outside China, a channel distinct from alleged chip smuggling. Malaysia has attracted more than $34 billion in data center investment, according to research cited by the Journal, with Chinese technology companies underpinning substantial demand.
The Journal said records showed Megaspeed arranged nearly $12 billion in advanced Nvidia

chip shipments to Chinese companies between March 2024 and June 2025. The documents did not establish how much equipment arrived or where it originated. Megaspeed said it complies with export rules and has hired outside lawyers to investigate. Nvidia
said it works to prevent smuggling.
The commercial stakes extend beyond Megaspeed. Singapore-based Aolani Cloud financed about $2.5 billion in Malaysian hardware, with ByteDance (
) as its anchor customer, the Journal reported. Nvidia
disclosed $12.4 billion in China revenue for the six months through July 26, although analysts believe overseas purchases create additional exposure to Chinese demand.

Commerce officials are developing restrictions covering Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore that could prohibit Chinese customers from remotely accessing certain advanced chips, according to the Journal. Malaysia is also investigating possible chip re-exports involving Megaspeed and its local affiliate.

title: Nvidia’s Southeast Asia business faces scrutiny over Chinese AI access
